label: Prostatic_Acinar_Adenocarcinoma
answer_markdown:
## Key Facts

- Most common malignancy of the prostate gland; arises from prostatic secretory (acinar) epithelium ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))
- Second most common cancer and second leading cause of cancer related death in American men ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))
- Typically multifocal; 75–80% arise in posterior/peripheral zone
- Absence of basal cell layer is pathognomonic; confirm with p63 and HMWCK IHC
- Graded via Gleason/ISUP Grade Group system (based on architecture)
- Key distinguishing features: infiltrative small acini, perineural invasion, glomerulations, collagenous micronodules, prominent nucleoli

## Terminology

- Prostatic acinar adenocarcinoma: invasive carcinoma derived from prostatic acini (usual/conventional adenocarcinoma)
- Synonyms: prostatic adenocarcinoma NOS, usual-type prostatic adenocarcinoma
- Distinct from ductal adenocarcinoma, which is a separate subtype
- Variants/subtypes: atrophic, pseudohyperplastic, microcystic, foamy gland, mucinous, signet ring-like, pleomorphic giant cell, sarcomatoid ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))
- ICD-O: C61.9; ICD-10: C61

## Essential and Desirable Diagnostic Criteria

- **Essential:**
  - Infiltrative small glands, lacking basal cell layer (confirm with p63 and HMWCK negativity) ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))
  - Enlarged round nuclei with prominent nucleoli
  - Pathognomonic features:  
    - Circumferential perineural invasion  
    - Glomerulations (glomeruloid bodies)  
    - Collagenous micronodules (mucinous fibroplasia)
  - Positive for at least one prostatic marker (PSA, PSAP, PSMA, NKX3.1)
  - AMACR (P504S) positive ([Gu Practical p221](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=221))
  - Gleason pattern and ISUP Grade Group reporting required (grading is architectural, not nuclear)  
- **Desirable:**
  - Intraluminal contents (nonexclusive): crystalloids, blue mucin, pink amorphous material ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))
  - Amphophilic cytoplasm
  - Growth pattern variants (atrophic, pseudohyperplastic, foamy gland, microcystic, mucinous, signet ring-like, pleomorphic giant cell, sarcomatoid)  
  - Molecular confirmation (ERG or TMPRSS2::ERG fusion) if available

## Etiology/Pathogenesis

- Originates from prostatic secretory (acinar) epithelium ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))
- Germline risk factors:
  - Age, race (higher in men of African heritage), family history
  - BRCA2 mutation (5x risk, younger onset, worse survival), HOXB13, Lynch syndrome, numerous SNPs
  - Obesity and high IGF1 also increase risk
- Somatic drivers: TMPRSS2::ERG fusion (most common), SPOP, FOXA1, IDH1, PTEN, TP53, MYC, ERG, ETV1/4, FLI1, CDH1 ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))
- High-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (HGPIN) is the putative precursor

## Clinical Issues

- **Epidemiology:**
  - Second most common cancer and second leading cause of cancer death in American men ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))
  - 92% diagnosed in US men age 55+, 19.5% age 75+
  - Found at autopsy in 40% of men over 60
  - Incidental prostate cancer in about 25% of cystoprostatectomies performed for treatment of bladder cancer
  - Highest age-standardized rates in Oceania, North America, Europe; lower in developing countries; higher in men of African heritage
- **Site:** 75–80% posterior/peripheral zone, 13–20% transition/periurethral zone ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))
- **Presentation:** Often asymptomatic unless locally advanced or metastatic; detected by raised PSA or DRE (may be enlarged, hard, asymmetrical)
- **Diagnosis:** Systematic needle core biopsies (TRUS/transperineal); prebiopsy MRI with targeted cores increases sensitivity; may be discovered incidentally in TURP or cystoprostatectomy; IHC (p63/HMWCK, AMACR) in equivocal cases
- **Treatment:** Stratified by risk (PSA, stage, grade, cribriform/intraductal pattern, perineural invasion); modalities include prostatectomy, external beam/seed radiotherapy, hormone therapy (LHRH analogues, antiandrogens); PSA monitoring post-surgery
- **Prognosis:** Varies by Gleason/ISUP Grade Group, tumor stage, margin status

## Staging

- TNM (AJCC):  
  - pT2: organ-confined  
  - pT3a: extraprostatic extension  
  - pT3b: seminal vesicle invasion ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))
- Gleason grading: architecture-based (patterns 3–5), summed for score, translated to ISUP Grade Group
- Percent ductal component in tumors with mixed acinar and ductal pattern is not prognostic ([Gu Prostate p275](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Prostate.pdf#page=275))

## Macroscopic

- Usually grossly inapparent; can form firm, cream-colored mass ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))
- Most tumors are multifocal

![Prostatectomy specimen](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/prostateprostaticCAgeneralZynger1.jpg)

## Microscopic

- Infiltrative, irregular small acini in desmoplastic stroma, lacking basal cell layer ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))
- Nuclei enlarged, round, prominent nucleoli
- Key pathognomonic features:
  - Circumferential perineural invasion  
    ![Perineural invasion](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/prostateadenoNOSshortvarma5.jpg)
  - Glomerulations (glomeruloid bodies)  
    ![Glomerulations](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/prostateadenoNOSshortvarma03.jpg)
  - Collagenous micronodules (mucinous fibroplasia)  
    ![Collagenous micronodules](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/prostateadenoNOSshortvarma19.jpg)
- Intraluminal contents: crystalloids, blue mucin, pink amorphous material  
  ![Crystals in gland lumens](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/prostateadenoNOSshortvarma20.jpg)
- Cytoplasm: amphophilic ([Gu Prostate p109](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Prostate.pdf#page=109))
- Variant patterns:  
  - Atrophic (mimics benign atrophy)  
    ![Atrophic variant of prostate cancer](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/prostateadenoNOSshortvarma07.jpg)
  - Pseudohyperplastic (branching, papillary, cystic glands)  
    ![Pseudohyperplastic variant of prostate cancer](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/prostateadenoNOSshortvarma09.jpg)
  - Foamy gland (abundant foamy cytoplasm)  
    ![Foamy gland variant of prostate cancer](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/prostateadenoNOSshortvarma13.jpg)
  - Microcystic, mucinous, signet ring-like, pleomorphic giant cell, sarcomatoid

## Ancillary Tests

- **IHC panel:**
  - PSA/PSAP (highly specific; may be focal in high-grade/treated cases) ([Gu Practical p1298](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=1298))
  - AMACR/P504S (highly sensitive, less specific)
  - Basal cell markers (p63, HMWCK): negative in carcinoma, positive in benign glands
  - Additional markers: NKX3.1, PSMA, prostein/p501s, ERG (by IHC or FISH)
  - ERG: highly specific for prostatic origin; not seen in adenosis ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenosis.html))
  - Rare cases show aberrant p63/HMWCK positivity ([Gu Prostate p133](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Prostate.pdf#page=133))
- **Molecular:**  
  - TMPRSS2::ERG fusion most common rearrangement
  - SPOP, FOXA1, IDH1, PTEN, TP53, MYC, ETV1/4, FLI1, CDH1

## Radiology

- Ultrasound used for biopsy guidance (not specific)
- MRI commonly for tumor localization and staging (PI-RADS/Likert)
- CT for nodes, bone scan for bony metastases, PET in selected cases ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))

- **ASAP:** Small crowded glands, insufficient for carcinoma, basal cells may be scant ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostatesuspicious.html))
- **Benign atrophy:** Bland, atrophic small glands, preserved basal cells, no nucleolar prominence
- **Adenosis:** Lobular small crowded glands, may have pale cytoplasm, basal cells, frequent corpora amylacea, AMACR can be focally positive ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenosis.html))
- **Seminal vesicle/Cowper gland:** Large, irregularly thick-walled or cystic glands, negative for prostate markers
- **High-grade PIN:** Retains at least focal basal cell layer, pre-existing gland structure, lacks infiltrative growth ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/GU/High_Grade_Prostatic_Intraepithelial_Neoplasia.html)), ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateHGPIN.html))
- **Urothelial carcinoma:** Marked pleomorphism, angulated nuclei, GATA3/thrombomodulin positive, prostate markers negative ([Gu Practical p1298](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=1298)), ([Gu Prostate p329](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Prostate.pdf#page=329))
- **Prostatic ductal adenocarcinoma:** Papillary/cribriform/tall columnar, typically no prominent nucleoli in PIN-like variant, negative for basal cells, more aggressive course ([Gu Prostate p273](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Prostate.pdf#page=273))
- **Adenosquamous carcinoma:** Mixture of adenocarcinoma and squamous areas, glandular component prostatic marker positive, squamous negative ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenosquamouscarcinoma.html))
- **Squamous cell carcinoma:** Keratinization, keratin pearls, intercellular bridges, absence of glandular differentiation ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/GU/Squamous_Cell_Carcinoma_Of_The_Prostate.html))
- **Adenoid cystic (basal cell) carcinoma:** Basaloid/cribriform/small solid nests, basal cell immunophenotype ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/GU/Adenoid_Cystic_Basal_Cell_Carcinoma_Of_The_Prostate.html))
- **Prostatic stromal sarcoma:** Malignant spindle cells, diffuse stromal growth, cytological atypia, CD34 and PR positive ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/GU/Prostatic_Stromal_Sarcoma.html))
- **Signet ring-like cell adenocarcinoma:** Tumor cells with compressed nuclei due to cytoplasmic mucin, >25% of tumor area ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostatesignet.html))
- **Nephrogenic adenoma:** Variety of growth patterns, tubules lined by bland cells, can mimic adenocarcinoma, weak/negative for PSA/PSAP ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostatenephrogenichyper.html))
- **Microcystic adenocarcinoma:** Abundant compact dilated cysts, prominent nucleoli and luminal crystalloid variable, lacks typical acinar features ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostatemicrocystic.html))
- **Pseudohyperplastic variant:** Large branching/papillary glands, can mimic benign hyperplasia, nucleoli prominent ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostatepseudoCA.html))
- **Atrophic adenocarcinoma:** Small crowded glands with atrophic cytoplasm, mimics benign atrophy ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateatrophic.html))

## Prognostic Factors

- Tumor volume (mm or % of core involved), Gleason score/ISUP Grade Group ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))
- Margin status, seminal vesicle/extraprostatic extension, perineural invasion
- Cribriform and intraductal carcinoma—adverse prognosis in invasive cancer
- Small cell component confers aggressive course
- Percent of ductal component in mixed acinar/ductal tumors is not prognostic ([Gu Prostate p275](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Prostate.pdf#page=275))

## Illustrative Cases

- 53-year-old man: prostate adenocarcinoma with retained basal cells in nodal metastases ([PathologyOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/prostateadenoNOS.html))
- 56-year-old man: metastatic prostate cancer with germline BRCA2 mutation
- 60-year-old man: supraclavicular node metastasis
- 64-year-old man: asymptomatic, oncocytic variant

- Diagnostic criteria language consistently distinguishes acinar adenocarcinoma from other subtypes

cards.title: Prostatic cystadenoma
cards.excerpt: Entity: Prostatic cystadenoma Section: microscopic Cysts are lined by a dual layer consisting of low columnar or atrophic secretory cells and flattened outer basal cells. Focal bland papillae may be seen. Cysts are surrounded by prostatic fibromuscular or fibrotic stroma, which may be hyalinized and show chronic inflammation. Squamous metaplasia may be seen in the lining epithelium. No marked epithelial atypia is present. By immunohistochemistry, the lining epithelium stains for PSA, PAP, and other prostate lineage–specific markers. Basal cells are decorated with high-molecular-weight cytokeratin and p63. Rarely, both high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia and acinar adenocarcinoma have been described as occurring in prostatic cystadenomas. Prostatic ductal adenocarcinoma can rarely present as a large multilocular mass resembling cystadenoma; however, prominent intracystic papillary growth and cytological atypia have been noted in cystadenocarcinoma.

cards.title: Adenosquamous carcinoma of the prostate
cards.excerpt: Entity: Adenosquamous carcinoma of the prostate Section: pathogenesis Most patients have a history of conventional prostatic adenocarcinoma for which they were treated by radiation and/or hormone therapy. --- The molecular background is comparable to that of conventional acinar adenocarcinoma, with TMPRSS2::ERG fusions, PTEN deletions, and SPOP mutations. In reported ERG-rearranged cases, immunohistochemical staining was strongly positive in the glandular component but weak to negative in the squamous component. One adenosquamous carcinoma with FAM131A::BRAF fusion has been reported.

cards.title: Squamous cell carcinoma of the prostate
cards.entity_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the prostate
cards.excerpt: Entity: Squamous cell carcinoma of the prostate Section: pathogenesis ERG activation at the posttranslational level. In contrast to the morphological features of SCC, which are nonspecific with respect to the site of origin, the presence of a TMPRSS2::ERG fusion essentially confirms the prostatic origin of the carcinoma. Also typical of acinar prostatic adenocarcinoma was the loss of PTEN in 3 cases, and a PTEN mutation was identified in the remaining case.

cards.title: Prostatic cystadenoma
cards.excerpt: Entity: Prostatic cystadenoma definition: Cystadenoma of the prostate is a benign epithelial neoplasm composed of multiple macroscopic cysts lined by bland prostatic secretory and basal cells and separated by fibrous or fibromuscular stroma. related_terminology: Acceptable: giant multilocular cystadenoma. essential_and_desirable_diagnostic_criteria: Essential: a large multiloculated cystic mass in or around the prostate gland; cysts lined by bland prostatic secretory and basal cells; no marked cytological atypia; septa with fibromuscular or fibrous stroma. Desirable: immunohistochemistry to confirm prostatic epithelial origin (if the differential diagnosis includes a seminal vesicle lesion).

cards.title: Adenoid cystic (basal cell) carcinoma of the prostate
cards.entity_name: Adenoid cystic (basal cell) carcinoma of the prostate
cards.excerpt: Entity: Adenoid cystic (basal cell) carcinoma of the prostate definition: Adenoid cystic (basal cell) carcinoma of the prostate is a malignant neoplasm thought to be derived from prostatic basal cells. related_terminology: Acceptable: adenoid cystic carcinoma; adenoid basal cell carcinoma; basal cell carcinoma of the prostate; adenoid cystic carcinoma (solid pattern). essential_and_desirable_diagnostic_criteria: Essential: basal cell morphology and immunophenotype; identification of malignant features (cytoarchitectural atypia, infiltration of non-neoplastic prostate, perineural invasion, necrosis); exclusion of metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma from a primary elsewhere, including the Cowper glands.

cards.title: High-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia
cards.excerpt: Entity: High-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia definition: High-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (HGPIN) is a proliferation of atypical secretory cells within prostatic glands. It is thought to be the earliest histologically recognizable precursor of invasive adenocarcinoma of the prostate. related_terminology: Acceptable: prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia. Not recommended: low-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia; grade 1, 2, or 3 prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia; carcinoma in situ. essential_and_desirable_diagnostic_criteria: Essential: crowded, stratified atypical secretory cells in pre-existing normal-sized or expanded glands; enlarged, hyperchromatic, and sometimes pleomorphic nuclei; prominent nucleoli; basal layer present but often discontinuous.

cards.title: Squamous cell carcinoma of the prostate
cards.entity_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the prostate
cards.excerpt: Entity: Squamous cell carcinoma of the prostate definition: Prostatic squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a rare type of prostate cancer with squamous histology, defined by keratinization, keratin pearls, and intercellular bridges. related_terminology: None essential_and_desirable_diagnostic_criteria: Essential: squamous architecture with keratinization and/or intercellular bridges; cellular anaplasia; absence of glandular differentiation; exclusion of prostatic adenocarcinoma with squamous differentiation, local invasion by bladder carcinoma with squamous features, and metastatic SCC.

cards.title: Prostatic stromal sarcoma
cards.excerpt: Entity: Prostatic stromal sarcoma definition: Prostatic stromal sarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumour that arises from the specialized prostatic stroma. related_terminology: Not recommended: cystosarcoma phyllodes. essential_and_desirable_diagnostic_criteria: Essential: diffuse stromal growth with hypercellularity, cytological atypia, increased or atypical mitosis, and necrosis; sarcomatoid prostate cancer and other sarcomas should be excluded. Desirable: immunohistochemistry positive for CD34 and PR.

cards.excerpt: Other patterns of prostatic duct adenocarcinoma, which by themselves may be difficult to identify as being of prostatic duct origin, may be seen in association with either the papillary or cribriform pattern. Occasionally, solid tumor masses with numerous thin-walled vessels distend prostatic ducts (Fig. 11.15). This pattern is a compact papillary form of prostatic duct adenocarcinoma, because areas can be seen where the solid pattern containing these thin fibrovascular cores open up into more recognizable papillary structures. cards.title: Adenocarcinoma — ICD-10: C61 - malignant neoplasm of the prostate
cards.excerpt:
Epidemiology
Second most common cancer and second leading cause of cancer related death in American men (SEER data available at NIH: Cancer Stat Facts - Common Cancer Sites [Accessed 10 December 2021])
92% of U.S. cases diagnosed in men aged 55+ years; 19.5% in men aged 75+ years (SEER data available at NIH: Cancer Stat Facts - Prostate Cancer [Accessed 10 December 2021])
Found at autopsy in 40% of men age 60+ years (J Natl Cancer Inst 2013;105:1050)
Incidental prostate cancer reported in about 25% of cystoprostatectomies performed for treatment of bladder cancer (J Urol 2017;197:385)
Globally, highest age standardized rates in Oceania, North America, Europe (World J Oncol 2019;10:63)
Lower rates in developing countries: may be due to different screening programs and diagnostic pathways
Higher incidence in men of African heritage (World J Oncol 2019;10:63)

cards.title: Adenocarcinoma — Sites
cards.excerpt:
Most tumors are multifocal (Eur Urol 2019;75:498)
75 - 80% are posterior / posterolateral peripheral zone
Approximately 13 - 20% are in transition (periurethral) zone (Prostate 1997;30:130, Urology 1994;43:11)
Most clinically significant cancers arise in the peripheral zone that is sampled by needle biopsies
Transition zone prostate cancer is associated with favorable pathologic features and better recurrence free survival (Prostate 2015;75:183)

cards.title: Adenocarcinoma — Etiology
cards.excerpt:
Obesity increases risk (Oncotarget 2018;9:34485)
Nonmodifiable risk factors: age, race and family history (Rev Urol 2002;4:S3)
Genetic susceptibility linked to African heritage (Rev Urol 2002;4:S3)
Increased risk with first degree relative with prostate cancer (Rev Urol 2002;4:S3)
BRCA2 mutations increase risk by 5 fold; BRCA2 associated cancers occur at a lower age and have worse survival outcomes (Saudi Med J 2020;41:9, Adv Anat Pathol 2020;27:11)
Additional germline variants associated with increased cancer risk occur in HOXB13 (Adv Anat Pathol 2020;27:11)
Increased risk in Lynch syndrome (Genet Med 2014;16:553)
Numerous single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that have a low to moderate effect on risk / progression have been identified (Am J Transl Res 2021;13:3868)
High levels of IGF1 may confer increased risk (Novartis Found Symp 2004;262:193)

cards.title: Adenocarcinoma — Highly penetrant variants occur in BRCA2 and HOXB13
cards.excerpt:
Over 280 SNPs have been identified as prostate cancer risk factors (Adv Anat Pathol 2020;27:11)
For most SNPs, the molecular mechanism of cancer association is generally unknown, as they occur in noncoding regions of the genome (Adv Anat Pathol 2020;27:11)
Somatic mutations occur in genes such as ERG, ETV1/4, FLI1, SPOP, FOXA1, IDH1, PTEN, TP53, MYC, CDH1 (Cell 2015;163:1011, Adv Anat Pathol 2020;27:11)
Most common somatic genomic rearrangement is fusion of the androgen regulated gene TMPRSS2 with a member of the ETS transcription family (Adv Anat Pathol 2020;27:11)
Somatic mutation profiles of prostate cancer are associated with clinical and pathological outcomes
There are 7 major subtypes, which are defined by either specific gene fusions of ETS transcription family members (ERG, ETV1, ETV4 and FLI1) or mutations (SPOP, FOXA1, IDH1) (Oncotarget 2018;9:14723)
Different subtypes have different molecular profiles, for example (Oncotarget 2018;9:14723):
ETS subset (59% of cases) are enriched in PTEN mutations
SPOP mutant subset (11%) of cases have distinct somatic copy number alteration profiles, including deletions of CHD1, 6q and 2q

missing_essentials: Epidemiology: Second most common cancer and second leading cause of cancer related death in American men (SEER data) — the draft only generally states '2nd most common cancer and cancer-related death', should specify US men as in the evidence.

Epidemiology/statistics: The draft gives percentage of diagnosis by age (92% diagnosed age 55+; 19.5% age 75+) but omits global distribution details—e.g., highest age-standardized rates in Oceania, North America, Europe; lower in developing countries; higher in African heritage.

Clinical Issues/Presentation: Incidental prostate cancer reported in about 25% of cystoprostatectomies performed for bladder cancer is not explicitly included (draft says only '25% incidental in cystoprostatectomy specimens', but not that it's specifically for treatment of bladder cancer).

Prognostic factors: The draft omits explicit mention that 'percent ductal component is not prognostic' for mixed acinar/ductal tumors, and that ductal morphology (not relevant for this entity per se, but comes up repeatedly in the differentials/literature).
redundant: prominent nucleoli' listed both under Essential and Desirable Diagnostic Criteria and again in Microscopic
'Amphophilic cytoplasm' is listed as both a desirable diagnostic feature and under Microscopic
